שמונה חודשים נלחם. וכמו תמיד - אף פעם לא התלונן. אוכלים טונה ותירס כל יום במשך חודשים - הכל בסדר. אין תחתונים להחלפה - לא נורא. מלחמה. הגיע הביתה אחרי 66 יום במלחמה - מכין לעצמו חביתה וטוסט בבוקר, וכנפיים וצ׳יפס בתנור בצהרים. בערב עשה כביסה לעצמו. ״אני בסדר, לא צריך כלום״. כששאלנו אותו איך זה להתמודד עם הדיסוננס של המלחמה האינטנסיבית והשקט בחדר עם סרט בטלוויזיה - ״מתרגלים״. בכל פעם שהגיע הביתה במהלך המלחמה, ולא היו יותר מדי פעמים - היה עייף. לפעמים קצת שפוף. אבל הכי שמח היה, כשחזר בבוקר לקראת הנסיעה להיפגש עם החברים שלו לפלוגה ולצאת למלחמה. אור היווה דוגמא לחיילים בפלוגה איך עובדים קשה בלי להתלונן, איך דבקים במשימה ומשלימים אותה גם בעייפות קיצונית, וגם איך ישנים בכל מצב, אם אפשר. אחרי מותו, יצרו איתנו קשר חברים בקבוצות אונליין בהן אור היה חבר. ידענו שהוא מדבר לפעמים באנגלית או עברית דרך האינטרנט, אבל לא ידענו מה. הוא לא סיפר ולא באמת ענה לשאלות. אפילו לא לחברים הקרובים. אותם נציגים שהגיעו אלינו סיפרו שהיה חבר בכמה קבוצות, שם מדברים אנשים מכל העולם על נושאים שונים. באחת הקבוצות היו מעל ל-36 אלף איש. אור היה בין 30 המנהלים וחבר מוערך מאוד על ידי כולם. בצ׳אט ההספד על אור שפתחו בקבוצות הללו היו מי שכתבו שיש כאלה שבוכים על מותו של אור גם במטרו בפאריז. עם האנגלית המצוינת שלו ובעזרת נימוקים מובנים ומשולבים עובדות וניתוחים היסטוריים, ובהתבסס על ההיכרות העמוקה שלו עם מלחמות בעולם - בנה נימוקים המסבירים את העמדה של ישראל אל מול האינטרסים של האויב וגרורותיו, ותפקד שם כנציג ההסברה של ישראל. גם אחרי תחילת המלחמה, בכל פעם שקיבל לידיו את הטלפון - חזר לקבוצות אלו כדי להגיב, להאיר את הדברים באור שלו. ציטוט מפי חבר לקבוצות האונליין: ״תמיד הרגשתי שאור בן פי שלושה מגילו האמיתי. כה חד, מבריק, בוגר, מלא חמלה וראיה חודרת מציאות. בגיל כה צעיר הוא הצליח להכיל, להבין ולהתמצא בכל כך הרבה מהמורכבויות של העולם, ולגעת בהרבה אנשים. כל מי שהכיר אותו אפילו לרגע, אומר שאור היה אחד האנשים ה-כ-י מצחיקים ונעימים שהכיר.״ חבר אחר באותן קבוצות אמר שאור ״לא לימד אותי רק על מלחמות, טנקים, ספורט, או ישראל - אלא לימד אותי גם על החיים״. אותו חבר, קצין בצבא ארה״ב, היה כפול מגילו של אור באותן שנים. אבל אור לא סיפר כלום. לא למשפחה, לא לחברי הילדות, לא לחבריו לפלוגה. הסתפקות במועט וצניעות קיצונית היו מאפיינים בולטים שלו, אבל היה בזה משהו מעבר לזה. היה בו איזשהו טוהר אמיתי. כאילו אמר - לא אכפת לי מה אומרים עלי - אני עושה את הדברים בשביל התוצאה. לא באמת מעניין אותי אם ידעו עלי חברים או משפחה כמה אני מצליח בצבא, בצלילה, בטיולים, בקבוצות האונליין. לא רוצה כיבודים, לא רוצה להתהדר בכלום- רוצה רק להשיג תוצאות. והוא השיג. אור תמיד הקיף עצמו בחברים. גם בתור ילד קטן במעוז אביב, גם במודיעין שם למד בבית ספר יסודי. מאז שהגיע לפרדס חנה, הייתה לו קבוצה מובחרת של חברים שבכל הזדמנות שיכל - הלך להיות איתם. לשחק כדורגל, לשתות בפאב, לאכול המבורגר, סמבוסק, או סתם לדבר ולהשתטות. חבריו כתבו עליו: ״בן אדם הכי צנוע שיש, חכם בצורה יוצאת דופן, ילד ערכי, הכי חברי שיש, הכי אכפתי, ושאפתן בצורה לא רגילה. הגעת אלינו ממודיעין בכיתה ז׳ וישר הקפת את עצמך בנו, ראית בנו משהו ואנחנו ראינו בך. לאורך השנים, מילדים קטנים - התבגרנו לאט לאט. אצלך זה הופיע בצבא. פתאום נהפכת לגבר-גבר. גידלת זקן שכולם אמרו שיפה לך, ומשהו בפנים טיפה השתנה. במהלך המלחמה, בכל פעם ששאלנו - שיתפת ואמרת שהכל בסדר ותחת שליטה. אני ברגוע. לא עובדים יותר מדי. אתה פשוט סמל הצניעות והעוז.״ בנובמבר נהרג בקרב חברו הטוב ינון תמיר. אור שמע על כך מטרנזיסטור ששימש אותם במהלך המלחמה בעזה. אחרי שחזר הביתה בפעם הראשונה מהמלחמה וביקר בקבר של ינון, כתב בפנקס שליווה אותו במהלך המלחמה תחת הכותרת ״להתמודד״: ״היה טוב בבית, אבל קשה. לראות את הקבר, להתפרק שם באמת בפּעם הראשונה מאז. קשה רצח. לא יודע איך חיים עם זה בשגרה, אני בקושי מצליח לחיות עם זה במלחמה עם התירוץ הנכון, כנראה, ש״הוא לא היה רוצה את זה״ …לפחות הוא לא סבל. פשוט נכבה האור…" עכשיו, שני החברים הטובים האלה קבורים אחד ליד השני. מילד קטן ועדין, סקרן, למדן, מצחיק ושנון; שעושה רק את מה שמעניין אותו, אבל עושה את זה הכי טוב, והרבה דברים עניינו אותו, התפתח גבר סקרן, למדן, מצחיק ושנון, וידען, דעתן, וחרוץ, וללא פחד. חזק — ועדין; קשוח — ורגיש; אדיש — ואכפתי; שמסור למשפחה, לחברים, לצבא, ולקבוצות האונליין שלו, שתמיד נלחם כדי להשיג מה שהוא רוצה, בדרך שלו, בשקט. באחת הפעמים שהגיע לתחנת הרכבת אחרי חופשה קצרה מהמלחמה, היה דוכן של ׳עזר מציון׳, ואור עצר שם לשמוע מהם מה הם עושים. בחפצים של אור שהגיעו אלינו מצאנו טופס בו חתם על תרומה חודשית ל׳עזר מציון׳. זה מה שיש לחייל במלחמה לעשות בדרך לעזה. למלא טופס תרומה חודשית לארגון עזרה לחולים ולאחרים. אור היה ילד, חייל, וגבר לתפארת. איש של ניגודים. ידען גדול בהיסטוריה, וידע מפליג בכדורגל לדורותיו. אוהד מושבע של ברצלונה והפועל ת״א בכדורגל, ומומחה על ב-NBA. ילד שיודע להתבודד, אבל חברותי וחברתי. איש רציני, אבל האדם הכי מצחיק שכל סובביו פגשו. ילד עדין ואדמוני שנראה תמים, וגבר חזק וקשוח שמתמודד עם קשיים כשהוא נושך שפתיים וממשיך. איש של שלום ופיוס, שהלך מתוך שליחות למלחמה שהאמין בצדקתה, וממנה לא שב. להקת ׳איפה הילד׳ הקליטה את השיר ׳אחרי המלחמה׳ לזכרו. המילים של השיר נכתבו על ידי אור בפנקס המלחמה שלו, תחת הכותרת ׳אחרי המלחמה׳, ונערכו על ידי חמי רודנר: ״אחרי המלחמה תמיד מדברים, צוחקים מה נעשה אחרי המלחמה לדפוק את הראש... ים, מסיבה כמו תכניות לחופשה רגילה הרגע הזה שאתה מתכנן להתאפס לאכול בריא להיכנס בראבק של עצמי בתכל׳ס מה מבטיח לך שתחזור חזרנו לעזה שלושה ימים בחוץ גשם סגול מתגעגע לחומוס של אבא, בעצם להכל שורה של קברים, הדור שלי את כולם – אני מכיר לא יודע איך חיים עם זה, אבל מעביר רגע הזה שאתה מתכנן להתאפס לאכול בריא להיכנס בראבק של עצמי בתכל׳ס מה מבטיח לך שתחזור״ והוא לא חזר. כשאור נולד - הוא לא נשם. כשאור הפסיק לנשום - אנחנו נותרנו בלי אוויר. סמל ראשון אור בלומוביץ נפל בקרב בשכונת תל סולטן בעזה ביום 15.6.2024. יחד עם עוד שבעה מחבריו לפלוגה באסון הנמר"ה. בן עשרים וחצי בנופלו. הוא הובא למנוחות בבית העלמין הצבאי בפרדס חנה. הותיר אחריו הורים ואח.

Or Blumouitz, son of Roni and Gill, was born on 7 September 2003 in Tel Aviv. He has a sister, Tal. When Or was born he was not breathing, and within seconds his sisters saved this adorable baby. Even as an infant he won hearts, and wherever he went people marveled at this wonder: quiet, smiling, curious. As a small child he could not manage to jump on two feet, and when he ran he often fell. But Or always fought to achieve what he wanted, in his own way, quietly. He trained and pushed himself until he succeeded, until he became good at it.

One of the things that most defined Or was his determination: persistence in everything he set out to do, even when it did not come easily. But some things did come easily, reading for example. A few days after starting first grade, he began reading books on his own; he read very fast and remembered everything. In fifth grade he was angry that the school curriculum taught only about the Holocaust and how many Jews were murdered in it, and not about the Second World War and the tens of millions who died in it. So he decided to learn about it himself. He read a great many books, watched documentaries, and not only remembered the details but could analyze the military and political moves of the war. Or also knew Israel's wars from the many books he read, from films, and from things he heard from his grandfathers, who had fought in Israel's wars. It was as if he was drawn to wars. But this was only one of his fields of interest. Or read, researched and checked every subject that interested him: general history and the history of the State of Israel, geopolitics, tanks, and sports. A great deal of sports. He also had a great love for very diverse music, like his other interests. The knowledge he gathered in his nearly twenty-one years was enormous.

When he was three he asked for a bar mitzvah gift of a diving course. At the age of twelve he took the course, and according to his instructor he was the best in a course of people around twenty years old. He had always been good in water, but from his very first dive it was clear there was no need to worry about him: he dove excellently, calmly and confidently. Or loved diving very much, and every two or three months he traveled to Eilat to dive. Dozens of one-day dives in Eilat showed us how this small, perfect diver grew, improved and got stronger. Or traveled a great deal from the age of a few months, even before he could walk, and he loved it very much. And as with everything he loved to do, he was really good at it. He joined scouting groups at a young age and stayed until he was eleven. He so enjoyed preparing for himself foxholes, covering himself with a plastic sheet and sleeping outdoors at night, without a tent, in the rain. He would return happy from such trips. As in many places, in the scouting groups too he was a magnet for children as an assistant instructor.

Or fought to become a combat soldier. He received a score of 97 despite a 20 cm platinum plate in his hand. The combat engineering training was not easy for him, and he also experienced failures, but he gritted his teeth and carried on. He continued and succeeded. In one training exercise the whole platoon was "wounded" except Or, who had to carry the wounded soldiers, each weighing about 90 to 100 kilos with equipment, to a certain point. Or carried the first, the second, the third and the fourth. He carried the fifth and then fell. After falling he went on dragging the mock casualty by crawling. At the end of the training he received the award for outstanding soldier. He did not talk about it in the army. He did not mention, for example, that he received a commendation in a winter training exercise in the battalion, an exercise the commanders at the time described as very difficult. He excelled and remained modest. He put his commendation certificate in a cupboard behind a pile of towels, and only when we took a towel out did we find the certificate. When we asked him about it he said, "Oh, just a training exercise, nothing serious." Afterwards he turned the certificate face down in the cupboard so that whoever took out more towels would not see it.

He never said no to a mission or a role he was asked to fill, in the battalion, on the front line, and in the war. Every task, as the soldiers and commanders told us, he carried out perfectly, and he went further, carrying out follow-up tasks even when not asked. According to his commanders, he was the best soldier in the company. He took on more and more areas of responsibility, and the company commander defined him as "the company's operations officer" — a role that does not formally exist, but he did it. The company commander wrote of him: "Blumo was the company's operations officer, the Kamav-Tz. There really is no such role; he simply created it. He lived it with his whole being. He was an officer in every sense and matter. Gifted, calculated, planning ahead, always knowing what was happening and where everyone was, what needed to be done… and alongside the genius and the image of the good boy, what a brave and daring fighter you were from the first battle. In every battle we were in, you would go out to operate the lethal weapon calmly and without any fear. I will never forget in my life the battle in the Jabalia area when we went out to attack and you went out to operate an obstacle. Suddenly two huge explosions, and I was sure something had happened to you. And you came down, quite calm, not at all matching the situation, and asked: 'Did you guys also hear the explosion?' After a few hours we understood we had been hit by a vehicle-borne explosive device, and miraculously nothing happened. And you continued as usual, under fire, going out, shooting and returning. What courage. You balanced me, Blumo. There was a calm and wisdom in you from which I learned again and again. A personal example of work ethic, one of the best I have met."

Beyond his role as a combat soldier operating a heavy machine gun, he was also a member of the combat engineering unit, flew operational drones during the war, and served as a company medic, although he had no medical training. He read about every subject he was required to handle, learned it, and excelled at it to such a degree that people said no one had ever performed better in any single role, and no one had performed all the roles together. In the war he served with courage, composure and calm, even under fire. He carried out his roles with a sense of mission, responsibility, and care for his fellow company members. But he did not tell anything at home, to friends, not even mention it. "How was it?" "Fine." "Was it hard?" "Not really."

Or was named after the character Or in Joseph Heller's *Catch-22*. Or, in the novel, was a fighter pilot in the war who crashed on every sortie. He crashed and came back, and everyone thought he was crazy to keep flying again and again. On the literary Or's final crash, he did not return. But the novel's main character, Yossarian, learned that Or had reached Sweden alive. Yossarian understood that all of Or's crashes had been training in physical and mental survival and in preparation for escaping the war. The Or of the book understood that this was his only way out of the war. Our Or trained for years, physically and mentally, in preparation for the war, and fought with complete knowledge that he was doing the right thing, and that together with all the members of his brave and excellent company they would win wherever they went. Or did not want war, and was angry at what led to it, but was proud to fight to protect the citizens of the State of Israel.

He fought for eight months, and as always, he never complained. Eating tuna and corn every day for months: all good. No spare underwear: not terrible. War. He came home after 66 days of war, making himself an omelette and toast in the morning, and chicken wings and chips in the oven at noon. In the evening he did his own laundry. "I'm fine, I don't need anything." When we asked him how it was to cope with the dissonance between intense war and the quiet of a room with a film on TV, he said, "You get used to it." Every time he came home during the war, and there were not many such times, he was tired. Sometimes a little down. But he was happiest when he returned in the morning before the drive to meet his company friends and go out to war again. Or set an example for the soldiers in the company of how to work hard without complaining, how to stick to a task and complete it even in extreme exhaustion, and how to sleep in any situation, when possible.

After his death, friends from the online groups in which Or had been a member contacted us. We knew he sometimes wrote in English or Hebrew online, but we did not know what. He did not talk about it and did not really answer questions, not even to close friends. The representatives who came to us told us he was a member of several groups, where people from all over the world discuss various topics. One of the groups had over 36,000 members. Or was among its 30 administrators and was highly valued by everyone. In the online chat condolences for Or that were opened in these groups, some wrote that there were people crying over Or's death even in the Paris metro. With his excellent English, and with well-structured arguments combining facts and historical analyses, and drawing on his deep knowledge of wars around the world, he built arguments explaining Israel's position against the interests of the enemy and its proxies, and served there as Israel's hasbara representative. Even after the war began, each time he got hold of a phone he returned to these groups to respond, to shed light on things in his own way.

A quote from a friend in the online groups: "I always felt Or was three times his real age. So sharp, brilliant, mature, full of compassion and a penetrating view of reality. At such a young age he managed to hold, understand and orient himself in so many of the world's complexities, and to touch many people. Everyone who knew him even for a moment says Or was one of the most, mo-st funny and pleasant people they knew."

Another friend from those groups said Or "didn't only teach me about wars, tanks, sports, or Israel, but also taught me about life." That friend, an officer in the U.S. Army, was twice Or's age in those years. But Or never told anything. Not to his family, not to his childhood friends, not to his company mates. Contentment with little and extreme modesty were prominent traits of his, but there was something beyond that. There was a real purity in him. As if he were saying: I don't care what people say about me; I do things for the result. It doesn't really matter to me whether friends or family know how successful I am in the army, in diving, in trips, in the online groups. I don't want honors, I don't want to flaunt anything. I only want to achieve results. And he did.

Or always surrounded himself with friends, even as a little boy in Ma'oz Aviv, and in Modiin, where he attended elementary school. Since arriving in Pardes Hanna he had a select group of friends, and whenever he could, he went to be with them: to play football, to drink in a pub, to eat a burger, sambusak, or just to talk and fool around. His friends wrote of him: "The most modest person there is, exceptionally wise, a valued boy, the most loyal friend, the most caring, and ambitious in an unusual way. You came to us from Modiin in seventh grade and immediately surrounded yourself with us. You saw something in us and we saw something in you. Over the years, from little children, we grew up slowly. With you it appeared in the army. Suddenly you became a real man. You grew a beard that everyone said looked good on you, and something inside you changed a little. During the war, every time we asked, you shared and said everything was fine and under control. I'm calm. We're not working too hard. You are simply the symbol of modesty and courage."

In November his close friend Yinon Tamir was killed in battle. Or heard about it on a transistor radio they used during the war in Gaza. After returning home for the first time from the war and visiting Yinon's grave, he wrote in the notebook that accompanied him during the war, under the heading "Coping": "It was good at home, but hard. To see the grave, to really break down there for the first time since. Murder is hard. I don't know how to live with it in routine. I barely manage to live with it in war, with the right excuse, apparently, that 'he wouldn't want this'… At least he didn't suffer. The light simply went out…"

Now these two good friends are buried side by side. From a small, gentle child, curious, studious, funny and witty, who did only what interested him but did it best, and was interested in many things, grew a man who was curious, studious, funny and witty, knowledgeable, opinionated, hardworking and fearless. Strong, and gentle; tough, and sensitive; indifferent, and caring; devoted to family, to friends, to the army, and to his online groups; a man who always fought to achieve what he wanted, in his own way, quietly.

On one of his returns to the train station after a short break from the war, there was a stand of Ezer Mitzion, and Or stopped there to hear what they were doing. Among Or's belongings that reached us we found a form he had signed for a monthly donation to Ezer Mitzion. That is what a soldier in the war does on the way to Gaza: fills in a form for a monthly donation to an organization that helps the sick and others. Or was a boy, a soldier, and a man to be proud of. A man of contradictions. A great expert in history and an encyclopedic knowledge of football across generations. A devoted fan of Barcelona and of Hapoel Tel Aviv in football, and an expert on the NBA. A boy who knew how to be alone, yet was friendly and sociable. A serious man, yet the funniest person everyone who met him knew. A gentle, freckled-faced boy who looked innocent, and a strong, tough man who faced difficulties by gritting his teeth and carrying on. A man of peace and reconciliation, who went to a war he believed in with a sense of mission, and from which he did not return.

The band "Eifo HaYeled" (Where Is the Boy) recorded the song "After the War" in his memory. The lyrics were written by Or in his war notebook under the heading "After the War," and were edited by Hami Rodner:

"After the war we always talk, laughing about what we'll do after the war, to bang our heads… sea, a party, like plans for a regular vacation. This moment you plan to rest, to eat healthy, to get back to yourself. Practically, what guarantees you'll come back? We returned to Gaza three days out, purple rain, missing Dad's hummus, basically everything. A row of graves, my whole generation — I know them all. I don't know how to live with it, but I carry this moment you plan to rest, to eat healthy, to get back to yourself. Practically, what guarantees you'll come back…"

And he did not come back.

When Or was born, he was not breathing. When Or stopped breathing, we were left without air.

Sergeant First Class Or Blumouitz fell in battle in the Tel Sultan neighborhood of Gaza on 15 June 2024, together with seven other members of his company in the Nimrod disaster. He was twenty-two and a half years old when he fell. He was laid to rest in the military cemetery in Pardes Hanna. He is survived by his parents and his sister.
